name: Fair Tax Foundation (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: shares of the result at the defaults by where the tax is paid: upper-middle income countries 50% (Repsol's split of its own income tax open to avoidance from its 2024 country-by-country report, Peru, Indonesia, Colombia, Brazil and Mexico, for its part, Libya's and Algeria's ring-fenced oil tax left out; Brazil and Mexico for Iberdrola's), high-income countries 50% (the UK 23%, Spain 15%, the US, Norway, Denmark, Finland, Sweden and the Netherlands 12%, by judgment from where the certified and indexed firms work); revenue in upper-middle income countries counts about seven times as much per dollar. The UK reporting campaign's 1% is in the UK.
summary: The Fair Tax Foundation, a UK not-for-profit community benefit society (not a registered charity; GBP 452,000 spent in 2025 and GBP 36,000 paid in interest to its member shareholders, 90% of its income fees from the businesses it certifies), runs the Fair Tax Mark, a certification of responsible tax conduct held by 275 businesses paying GBP 4.1 billion a year in corporate income tax, an index benchmarking 21 multinationals that pay over EUR 30 billion, and campaigns for public country-by-country reporting in the UK. An average year of its spending since 2014 (about three fifths of 2025's in real terms) is counted against the tax those firms would otherwise avoid that the mark and the index remove (judged 15% and 2% of a judged 3% avoided), for the years a won reform counts less firms dropping out, and against a small share of a chance that the UK adopts public reporting. The tax is valued as public revenue spread over citizens' consumption where it is paid, net of what it costs the richer people who pay it; the eighth paid in Brazil, Peru, Mexico and other upper-middle income countries (from Repsol's own country-by-country report and a judgment for Iberdrola) counts about seven times as much per dollar and is half the result. With the next dollar at 40% of the average (fees pay for certification, so a gift funds the advocacy), it comes to about {{result}} years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars. The result is mostly uncertainty: how much tax certified firms would have avoided and how much the mark changed are unmeasured, the model's own ranges span over two-hundred-thousandfold, and every branch is discounted by the shared missing-data slider.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: An average year of what the Fair Tax Foundation spent since 2014, from its accounts (2022-2025) and grant disclosures (2017-2021) in 2025 prices, with judged earlier years, against 2025's GBP 451,698. The society is a not-for-profit community benefit society registered with the Financial Conduct Authority (no. 32308R), with an asset lock: not a registered charity, so gifts get no Gift Aid. Ninety per cent of its income is fees from the businesses it certifies; it accepts donations (GBP 148 in 2025). Its accounts are exempt from audit and checked by an independent reporting accountant.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: The corporate tax the three outcomes concern: what the businesses holding the Fair Tax Mark pay each year, what the multinationals on its Tax Responsibility and Transparency Index pay, and the UK large businesses' corporation tax that public country-by-country reporting would cover.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What share of that tax the work adds, and what a dollar of it is worth: public revenue spread over citizens' consumption where it is paid, less what the tax costs those who pay it. Certification and benchmarking count the years a won reform counts, less firms that drop out; the UK reporting law is a chance, after a wait.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Each branch's share of the credit, trust in the chain, missing data and side effects; the canonical rows are their outcome-weighted averages, for reading only.

sections.title: Value of a dollar moved (shared)
sections.explainer: charityevals' shared method for money a meta charity moves, the same rows in every such model (docs/normalization.md 2.8). A dollar moved is worth what the charities it reaches achieve, each at its live result on this site under your values; new money counts in full, shifted money only for the gain over where it would have gone.

sections.title: Career changes
sections.explainer: People the charity moves into high-impact jobs: per career changed, the pay they give up for the years they stay, valued at the new employer's live result per dollar, times the share of changes the charity caused (docs/normalization.md 2.8). The mirror of staff pay below market.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The three branches' credited value, spread over the 12 years of work since 2014, per dollar of an average year's spending.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

story.sentence: $1,000 buys **{1000 / cost_total|%} of a year of the Fair Tax Foundation's work**, pushing businesses to **pay more of the tax they owe**.

rows.label: Consumption per person of those who pay the extra tax, as a multiple of the UK average
rows.explainer: The shared figure for those who bear corporate income tax (@public_funds.corporate_tax_payer_multiple): about three quarters on shareholders, mostly rich households and pension funds, and a quarter on workers, who consume about the average, so 2.5 times UK household consumption per person (1.5 to 4). The certified firms (co-operatives, building societies and family firms beside listed multinationals) pay ordinary corporate tax, so their payers are the same.

rows.label: Cost to the payers of a dollar of tax, units of value
rows.explainer: Domestic money's rule (docs/normalization.md 2.20): a dollar taken from someone consuming c costs 1/c in ln(consumption), valued at the shared rate, times the shared marginal cost of public funds (@public_funds.mcpf).

rows.label: Value of a dollar of UK public revenue, net of its payers' cost, units of value
rows.explainer: Its known use: UK public spending, spread over everyone's consumption (1/c per dollar on the log scale at the UK average), less the payers' cost. About a hundredth of cash per dollar.

rows.label: Value of a dollar of revenue in an upper-middle income country, net of its payers' cost, units of value

rows.label: Share of these firms' corporate income tax they would avoid without the mark or index

source.title: HM Revenue and Customs, Measuring tax gaps 2026 edition: tax gap estimates for 2024 to 2025, chapter 5, Corporation Tax (23 June 2026)
source.quote: The tax gap for large businesses Corporation Tax is 4.3% of the large businesses theoretical Corporation Tax liability

rows.explainer: Anchors: HMRC's corporation tax gap for UK large businesses is 4.3% of their liability (mid-sized 5.9%), counting disputed legal interpretation and evasion against HMRC's reading of the law but not legal profit shifting; Tørsløv, Wier and Zucman estimate profit shifting costs about a tenth of corporate tax revenue worldwide, more in high-tax European countries. Firms that seek the mark or the index are self-selected as responsible taxpayers (the 2025 accounts, p. 5: the society focuses on recognising business that pays the right amount of tax), so judged 3% (1% to 10%), below both anchors.

rows.label: Share of their avoidance gap that firms named in a public campaign gave up

source.title: Dyreng, Hoopes and Wilde (2014), Public pressure and corporate tax behaviour, Oxford University Centre for Business Taxation working paper 14/16 (published 2016, Journal of Accounting Research 54(1), 147-186)
source.quote: Specifically, our estimates suggest a 3.7 percentage point increase in the effective tax rates (ETRs) of noncompliant firms relative to the effective tax rates of compliant firms in the years following the initial public pressure to comply.

rows.explainer: The FTSE 100 firms ActionAid named for not disclosing their subsidiaries raised their effective tax rates by 3.7 points against the other firms; before the pressure their unadjusted rates averaged 29.3% against the others' 32.5% (footnote 22), a 3.2-point gap. Under strong, targeted public pressure the named firms gave up about all of their avoidance relative to their peers. Judged 90% (40% to 100%) for the estimate's own uncertainty.

rows.label: Certification: the mark's effect on avoidance as a share of a targeted campaign's
rows.explainer: A voluntary standard that firms choose is much weaker than a campaign against named avoiders: many certified firms already met most of it and changed little (often only publishing their policy), and the mark allows low tax where reporting is full. Its pull is that firms want to keep it: the standard requires a published policy shunning avoidance and the artificial use of tax havens, country-by-country reporting by multinationals and yearly reassessment. Judged 17% (3% to 45%) of the campaign's effect: about 15% of the avoidance removed at the defaults.

rows.label: Certification: share of that avoidance the mark removes
rows.explainer: What firms under a campaign's pressure gave up, scaled for a voluntary standard. Whether the change would have come anyway later is the years counted (Convention 5).

rows.label: Benchmarking: the index's effect on avoidance as a share of certification's
rows.explainer: The index scores a firm against civil-society frameworks and pending laws in five areas of tax conduct and sets no pass mark; firms that pay for it are already working on their tax conduct, and its first full year was 2025. Judged 15% of certification's effect (3% to 50%), as nothing has to change: about 2% of the avoidance at the defaults.

rows.label: Certification: share of the certified tax open to avoidance that is paid in upper-middle income countries
rows.explainer: The society publishes no country split; most of the tax is Repsol's and Iberdrola's, certified in 2024 (2024 accounts, p. 4: the tax rose from GBP 1.7 billion to 5.3 billion with the new certifications). Repsol's own report puts EUR 684 million of its EUR 1,530 million income tax accrued in 2024 in upper-middle income countries, but EUR 484 million of it is Libya's and Algeria's ring-fenced upstream oil tax, paid at the nominal rate beside the national oil companies, with no avoidance for the mark to remove; the rest (Peru 83, Indonesia 70, Colombia 30, Brazil 16, Mexico 1) is about 4% of the certified EUR 4.8 billion. Bolivia's accrual is negative, so none in lower-middle income countries. Iberdrola, about another third, has large businesses in Brazil (Neoenergia) and Mexico; its own tax reports could not be read here (its site refuses automated downloads), so its share there is judged at about a quarter, adding about 8%. The many UK-only firms pay none. Judged 13% (7% to 25%) of the tax open to avoidance, each dollar valued where the tax is now paid.

source.title: Repsol, 2024 Country by Country Tax Report
source.page: p. 12, CbCr 2024 reported data, income tax accrued (EUR million)

rows.label: Certification: tax certified over the years as a multiple of that still certified in 2025
rows.explainer: The 2025 figure counts only firms still certified. Few have left: the businesses covered rose from 250 (2023) to 270 (2024) to 275 (2025) with 12 and 8 new parent companies, and before 2024 the certified tax was only GBP 1.7 billion (2024 accounts, p. 4), so lapsed tax is a small share of today's GBP 4.1 billion; the fall from GBP 5.3 billion in 2024 is mostly the two Spanish firms' tax moving with energy prices, not lapses. Judged 1.1 (1.02 to 1.3): the yearly flow of certifications is the tax ever certified spread over the years (Convention 3).

Tax-weighted, few have left (the large early holders such as SSE remain; see a_lapsed_adj). Judged 3% a year (1% to 10%), counted beside the discount rate like the shared repeal rate for won reforms.

rows.label: Benchmarking: chance the change happens
rows.explainer: 1: the benchmarking is done; whether it changed anything is c_changed_share.

rows.label: Benchmarking: discounted years counted
rows.explainer: As certification: the shared years and rate, with the same yearly drop-out.

rows.label: Benchmarking: value over the years counted, units of value
rows.explainer: Before the society's share and adjustments.

rows.label: Policy: extra corporation tax public country-by-country reporting would raise, as a share of large businesses' liability
rows.explainer: The society campaigns for the UK to require multinationals to publish their profit and tax country by country, as the EU has since 2024 and Australia plans (2023 accounts, p. 8). Evidence from the EU's public reporting for banks is mixed: Overesch and Wolff (2021, Contemporary Accounting Research 38(3)) find banks exposed in tax havens raised their tax expense; Joshi, Outslay and Persson (2020, Contemporary Accounting Research 37(4)) find less income shifting but no robust change in effective tax rates. The UK's large-business gap is 4.3% and the global minimum tax already covers the same firms. Judged 1% of the large businesses' liability (0.1% to 5%).

rows.label: Certification: the society's share of the resources behind the change
rows.explainer: Coalition credit by resources (Convention 2), among those who press firms towards the mark: the pressure that makes them want it comes partly from others (the Tax Justice Network and other campaigns, the press). The firms' own tax and finance staff, who do the work of changing policies and reporting, are the adopters: their part is under the mobiliser's share, not in this one (docs/normalization.md 2.24). The fees the firms pay are the society's own income and spending, already in its cost. Judged 70% (45% to 90%).

source.title: Fair Tax Foundation Limited, Directors' report and financial statements for the year ended 31 December 2024 (unaudited, audit exemption)
source.quote: The number of Fair Tax councils increased from 56 to 63, nearly all additions passing resolutions with unanimous cross-party support.

rows.explainer: The mark sets a public benchmark: 63 councils (with about GBP 28 billion of outside spending a year) have passed the Councils for Fair Tax Declaration, Fair Tax Week and the society's polling and briefings reach firms and investors, and some firms adopt the standard's policies without applying. Judged a fifth of the branch (0 to 1).

rows.label: Side effect: revenue lost in low-tax countries when profits move back, as a share of the branch
rows.explainer: Part of the extra tax is profit no longer booked in low-tax countries (Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands), which lose that revenue; they are rich and the rates low, so the loss is small. Judged -5% (-20% to 0).

rows.label: Side effect: avoidance the mark shields from scrutiny, as a share of the branch
rows.explainer: A certified firm that keeps some avoidance may face less scrutiny from the press, campaigners and customers because it holds the mark. Judged -5% of the branch (-20% to 0): the standard is reassessed yearly and asks for full reporting, which limits it.

rows.label: Certification: side effects, as a share of the branch
rows.explainer: The branch's side effects summed.

rows.label: Benchmarking: the society's share of the resources behind the change
rows.explainer: As certification (a_attribution_share_shared, 0.7), lower because the index was developed and is run with CSR Europe (2024 accounts, p. 5). Judged 55% (30% to 80%).

rows.label: Benchmarking: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The share among co-advocates times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Benchmarking: trust in the chain
rows.explainer: As certification (0.65), lower: two years old, no pass mark and no follow-up of the indexed firms' tax. Judged 0.5 (0.2 to 0.8).

rows.label: Benchmarking: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: in c_changed_share and the years counted (Convention 5).

rows.label: Benchmarking: discount for missing data
rows.explainer: Thin (Convention 12): no measured change in the indexed firms' tax; the shared slider.

rows.label: Benchmarking: total adjustment
rows.explainer: The branch's adjustments multiplied.

rows.label: Benchmarking: side effects, as a share of the branch
rows.explainer: The same revenue lost in low-tax countries as for certification; no spillover beyond the indexed firms is counted for so new a product.

rows.label: Policy: the society's share of the UK campaign's resources
rows.explainer: Coalition credit by resources (Convention 2): the Tax Justice Network, Tax Justice UK, Oxfam, Christian Aid, ActionAid and investor groups also press for public reporting, with far larger budgets; the society's own grant for this work was GBP 3,504 a year (Funding for Social Change, grant disclosure 2023-2025), beside staff time. Judged 4% (1% to 10%).

The UK government that would decide is the adopter, under the mobiliser's share, not in this one (docs/normalization.md 2.24); the EU's and Australia's laws and the OECD's rules are in the chance (b_issue_record_adj and the shared base rate), not here. Judged 80% (50% to 100%).

rows.explainer: Thin (Convention 12): no measure of the society's part; the shared slider.
